\title{The CRT-Multiplicative Free-Witness Classification\\ and the Trace Lemma}
\author{Aristotle}
\date{14 August 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
A \emph{free witness} for a semiprime modulus $N = pq$ is a single integer $W(N)$, defined
without reference to the factorization, from which the factorization can nevertheless be
recovered in polynomial time. Nine structurally unrelated constructions --- modular circle
counts, $k$-th root counts, binary quadratic form representation numbers, Heisenberg class
counts, cusp indices, zeta-linear-programming aggregates, code-distance witnesses,
congruence-divisor witnesses, and divisor power sums --- have been observed to have this
property. We prove that they are instances of a single mechanism: a counting aggregate over a
Chinese-Remainder-separable domain whose local weight is CRT-multiplicative and
non-polynomial.

We establish four groups of results. (i) \emph{Layer one, proved.} For coprime moduli $m,n$, a
weight $f(x) = A(x \bmod m)B(x \bmod n)$ has aggregate
$\sum_{x<mn} f(x) = (\sum_{a<m}A(a))(\sum_{b<n}B(b))$; and splitting through the CRT is
\emph{equivalent}, for a nowhere-vanishing weight over a field, to a four-point rank-one
identity, making membership in the class a finite, decidable test. (ii) \emph{The Trace
Lemma.} A CRT-multiplicative witness with affine-power local weight $w(x) = ax^k+c$ satisfies
$ac(p^k+q^k) = W(N) - a^2N^k - c^2$; the resulting power sum, with $N$, determines $\{p,q\}$
uniquely, and the three observed recovery channels (trace, larger factor, residue/order
vector) are each complete. (iii) \emph{Rigidity.} For $k \ge 1$ and $c \ne 0$, no integer
polynomial agrees with such a witness on all odd semiprimes. (iv) \emph{A validated prediction
and a sharp boundary.} The divisor power sum $\sigma_k$, predicted by the classification, is
confirmed as a free witness with the explicit trace formula
$p+q = \sqrt{\sigma_2(N)+2N-1-N^2}$; truncated weights provably leave the class; exponential
phase weights are shown to \emph{split} through the CRT after all --- correcting the standard
justification --- and to fail instead by non-locality of the B\'ezout twist. We further prove a
2-adic sealing dichotomy ($\sigma_{2j}(N) \equiv 2 + 2N^{2j} \bmod 64$ always; an explicit
separation at $128$) and identify an unnoticed second information channel: for odd squarefree
$N$, the 2-adic valuation of $\sigma_{2j}(N)$ equals $\omega(N)$.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} Chinese Remainder Theorem; multiplicative functions; divisor power
sums; integer factorization; rank-one decomposition; 2-adic valuation; Dirichlet characters.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The phenomenon}

Let $N = pq$ be a product of two distinct odd primes and let
\[
  C(N) = \#\{(x,y) \in (\mathbb{Z}/N)^2 : x^2+y^2 \equiv 1 \pmod N\}
\]
be the number of points on the modular unit circle. For distinct odd primes,
\[
  C(pq) = \bigl(p - \chi_p(-1)\bigr)\bigl(q - \chi_q(-1)\bigr),
\]
where $\chi_p(-1) = +1$ if $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $-1$ if $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. If
$p \equiv q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ the local weights are $p+1$ and $q+1$, so
\[
  C(N) = (p+1)(q+1) = N + (p+q) + 1, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad p+q = C(N) - N - 1 .
\]
The scalar $C(N)$ therefore encodes the trace $s = p+q$; with $N = pq$ known, $p$ and $q$ are
the roots of $x^2 - sx + N$. We call such a scalar a \emph{free witness}: its definition
mentions only $N$, yet its value determines the factorization. Nine structurally distinct
constructions with this property have been catalogued, drawing on Kronecker symbols,
multiplicative orders, divisor sums, class counts and code distances. Each was found
independently. This paper proves that they are a single object.

\subsection{The mechanism}

Every member of the family has three layers. \emph{(1) CRT decomposition:} the counting domain
is separable, $S_N \cong S_p \times S_q$. \emph{(2) A non-polynomial local weight:} the count
factors as $W(N) = w(p)w(q)$, where $w$ depends on a single prime through an arithmetic
function. \emph{(3) Sealing:} the closed form requires the factors, and the only factor-free
evaluation route is enumeration of the CRT-product domain, at cost $\Theta(N)$ or
$\Theta(N^2)$. Layers 1 and 2 make the scalar a key; layer 3 keeps it locked. Layers 1 and 2,
and the consequences of layer 3's failure modes, are proved here; the necessity of layer 3's
cost is equivalent to the hardness of factoring and is not.

\section{Definitions}

Throughout, $p,q$ denote distinct odd primes, $N = pq$, and $\omega(N)$ the number of distinct
prime factors of $N$. For $k \ge 0$, $\sigma_k(N) = \sum_{d \mid N} d^k$, and $\vtwo$ is the
2-adic valuation.

\begin{definition}[CRT-multiplicative semiprime witness]
A \emph{semiprime witness} is a pair of functions $W : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$ (the
\emph{aggregate}, a function of the modulus alone) and $w : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$ (the
\emph{local weight}, a function of a single prime), subject to the single axiom
\[
  W(pq) = w(p)\,w(q) \qquad \text{for all distinct odd primes } p \ne q .
\]
\end{definition}

The definition says nothing about \emph{how} $W$ is computed; the classification is a statement
about the shape of the local weight only, which is what allows nine constructions to be treated
at once.

\begin{definition}[Affine-power shape]
A local weight has \emph{affine-power shape} with data $(a,k,c)$ if $w(x) = ax^k+c$ on the
primes under consideration. The case $a = 1$, $c \ne 0$ is the \emph{power shape}; $a = c = 1$
is the \emph{unit} case, covering the divisor power sums and, for Blum primes, the circle count.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Splitting through the CRT]
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $m,n \ge 1$. A weight $f:\mathbb{N}\to R$ \emph{splits
through the CRT at $(m,n)$}, written $f \in \Split(m,n)$, if there exist $A,B$ with
$f(x) = A(x \bmod m)\,B(x \bmod n)$ for all $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Free witness]
A semiprime witness is a \emph{free witness} if (i) it is \emph{factoring-complete} --- the pair
$\{p,q\}$ is determined in polynomial time by $W(N)$ and $N$ --- and (ii) it is
\emph{non-polynomial} --- no $P \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ satisfies $W(pq) = P(pq)$ for all distinct
odd primes.
\end{definition}

\section{Layer one: separability and the rank-one criterion}

\begin{theorem}[Aggregate multiplicativity]\label{thm:aggregate}
Let $m,n \ge 1$ be coprime and $A,B : \mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$. Then
\[
  \sum_{x=0}^{mn-1} A(x \bmod m)\,B(x \bmod n)
  \;=\; \Bigl(\sum_{a=0}^{m-1} A(a)\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{b=0}^{n-1} B(b)\Bigr).
\]
Consequently, if $f \in \Split(m,n)$ with witnesses $A,B$, then
$\sum_{x<mn} f(x) = (\sum_{a<m}A(a))(\sum_{b<n}B(b))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Expand the right-hand side as a double sum over $[0,m)\times[0,n)$. The map
$x \mapsto (x \bmod m, x \bmod n)$ is a bijection from $[0,mn)$ onto that product, with inverse
$(a,b)\mapsto \crt(a,b) \bmod mn$. That the maps are mutually inverse is CRT existence and
uniqueness: $\crt(x \bmod m, x \bmod n) \equiv x$ modulo $m$ and modulo $n$, hence modulo $mn$
by coprimality, hence equals $x$ after reduction; conversely, reducing the lift modulo $m$
recovers $a$ and modulo $n$ recovers $b$. Reindexing along this bijection gives the identity.
\end{proof}

This is layer one, in full generality: \emph{CRT-separable domain $+$ CRT-multiplicative weight
$\Rightarrow$ the count factors}.

\begin{theorem}[Rank-one necessity]\label{thm:rankone}
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $f \in \Split(m,n)$. If $x,y,z,w$ satisfy the
\emph{crossing conditions}
\[
  z \equiv x \ (m), \quad z \equiv y \ (n), \quad w \equiv y \ (m), \quad w \equiv x \ (n),
\]
then $f(x)f(y) = f(z)f(w)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Substituting $f(t) = A(t \bmod m)B(t \bmod n)$, both sides equal
$A(x)B(x)A(y)B(y)$ after commuting factors.
\end{proof}

A single violating quadruple refutes CRT-multiplicativity: four evaluations decide a candidate.

\begin{theorem}[Four-point characterization]\label{thm:fourpoint}
Let $K$ be a field, $m,n$ coprime, and $f : \mathbb{N}\to K$ with $f(0)\ne 0$. Then
$f \in \Split(m,n)$ \emph{if and only if} the rank-one identity of
Theorem~\ref{thm:rankone} holds for all quadruples satisfying the crossing conditions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Necessity is Theorem~\ref{thm:rankone}. For sufficiency define the axis profiles
$A(a) = f(\crt(a,0))$ and $B(b) = f(\crt(0,b))/f(0)$, legitimate since $f(0)\ne 0$. Fix $x$ and
apply the hypothesis to $(x,\,0,\,\crt(x\bmod m,0),\,\crt(0,x\bmod n))$, whose crossing
conditions hold by the defining congruences of the lift:
$f(x)f(0) = A(x\bmod m)B(x\bmod n)f(0)$. Divide by $f(0)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Decidability of class membership]
For a nowhere-vanishing weight on $\mathbb{Z}/mn$ over a field, membership in the
CRT-multiplicative class is decided by the rank-one identity on the $O(m^2n^2)$ crossed
quadruples --- indeed, by the $mn$ quadruples anchored at $0$. The question ``is this experiment
a free witness?'', previously answered case by case, becomes an algorithm.
\end{corollary}

\section{The Trace Lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Trace Lemma, affine-power form]\label{thm:trace}
Let $(W,w)$ be a semiprime witness and $p \ne q$ distinct odd primes with $w(p) = ap^k+c$ and
$w(q) = aq^k+c$. Then, with $N = pq$,
\[
  a\,c\,(p^k+q^k) \;=\; W(N) - a^2N^k - c^2 .
\]
In particular for $a=1$, $c \ne 0$, $\;p^k+q^k = (W(N)-N^k-c^2)/c$; and for $a=c=1$,
$\;p^k+q^k = W(N)-N^k-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$W(N) = (ap^k+c)(aq^k+c) = a^2(pq)^k + ac(p^k+q^k) + c^2$; rearrange.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Trace]
With $k=1$, $a=c=1$: $p+q = W(N)-N-1$. For the circle witness at Blum pairs this is
$p+q = C(N)-N-1$; for $\sigma_1$ it is $p+q = \sigma(N)-N-1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Trace square]\label{cor:tracesq}
With $k=2$, $a=c=1$: since $(p+q)^2 = p^2+q^2+2N$, one has $(p+q)^2 = W(N)-N^2+2N-1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Sum and product determine the pair]\label{thm:pair}
Let $p,q,p',q'$ be non-negative integers with $p' \ne 0$, $pq = p'q'$ and $p+q = p'+q'$. Then
$(p',q') = (p,q)$ or $(p',q') = (q,p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$(p'-p)(p'-q) = p'^2 - (p+q)p' + pq = p'^2 - (p'+q')p' + p'q' = 0$, so $p' \in \{p,q\}$; in the
first case cancel $p'\ne0$ in the product relation, in the second use the sum relation.
\end{proof}

Equivalently, $p,q$ are the roots of $X^2 - sX + N$ with $s = p+q$: the witness value is not
evidence about the factorization but a re-encoding of it.

\subsection*{The three recovery channels}

\begin{proposition}[Trace $\Rightarrow$ larger factor]\label{prop:max}
For $p \le q$, $\;2q = (p+q) + \bigl\lfloor\sqrt{(p+q)^2-4pq}\bigr\rfloor$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $q = p+d$; then $(p+q)^2-4pq = d^2$ exactly, so the integer square root is $d$ and
$(p+q)+d = 2q$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Larger factor $\Rightarrow$ factorization]
If $pq = N$ with $q \ne 0$ then $p = N/q$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Residue channel]
If $p,p' < M$ and $p \equiv p' \pmod M$ then $p = p'$.
\end{proposition}

The last proposition is why the residue/order-vector witnesses of the family are recoverable: a
residue pins the factor as soon as its modulus exceeds it. Combining
Theorems~\ref{thm:trace}, \ref{thm:pair} and Propositions~\ref{prop:max}ff.: every recoverable
witness in the family carries exactly one factor-secret coordinate --- $p+q$, or $\max(p,q)$,
or a residue/order vector --- and each determines the factorization in polynomial time. On
semiprimes that is the whole information content; \S\ref{sec:omega} shows the semiprime
restriction was hiding a second channel.

\section{Rigidity: the polynomial barrier}

\begin{proposition}[Difference test]\label{prop:diff}
Let $W:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z}$, $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, and $N_1,N_2 \in S$ with
$(N_1-N_2) \nmid (W(N_1)-W(N_2))$. Then no $P \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ satisfies $W(n) = P(n)$ for all
$n \in S$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $P \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ and integers $a,b$ one has $a-b \mid P(a)-P(b)$, since
$a-b \mid a^j-b^j$ termwise.
\end{proof}

For instance $C(21) = 32$, $C(15) = 16$ and $6 \nmid 16$; and $\sigma_2(33) = 1220$,
$\sigma_2(15) = 260$, $18 \nmid 960$.

\begin{theorem}[No polynomial formula, all exponents]\label{thm:rigidity}
Let $(W,w)$ be a semiprime witness with $w(s) = s^k+c$ for every odd prime $s$, where $k \ge 1$
and $c \ne 0$. Then there is no $P \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ with $W(pq) = P(pq)$ for all distinct odd
primes $p \ne q$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Suppose such a $P$ exists and fix an odd prime $r$. For every odd prime $q \notin \{r,2\}$,
$P(rq) = w(r)w(q) = (r^k+c)(q^k+c)$. Both sides are polynomials in one variable evaluated at
$q$, and they agree at infinitely many integers, so they are equal as polynomials:
\[
  P(rX) = (r^k+c)(X^k+c) \quad\text{in } \mathbb{Z}[X].
\]
Take $r=3$, evaluate at $X = 10$; take $r=5$, evaluate at $X=6$. Both give $P(30)$:
\[
  (3^k+c)(10^k+c) = P(30) = (5^k+c)(6^k+c).
\]
The leading terms agree ($3^k10^k = 30^k = 5^k6^k$) and the constants agree, leaving
$c(10^k+3^k) = c(6^k+5^k)$. Cancelling $c \ne 0$ gives $10^k+3^k = 6^k+5^k$, false for $k \ge 1$:
for $k = 1$, $13 \ne 11$; for $k \ge 2$, induction gives $2\cdot 6^k \le 10^k$, whence
$6^k+5^k \le 2\cdot6^k \le 10^k < 10^k+3^k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The forced identity is $c(10^k+3^k) = c(6^k+5^k)$, so a polynomial closed form would require
$c = 0$, i.e.\ a homogeneous local weight $w(x) = x^k$ whose aggregate is the polynomial $N^k$
and which carries no factor information. A nonzero constant term in the local weight is exactly
what obstructs a polynomial closed form, and exactly what places $p^k+q^k$ in the aggregate:
the Trace Lemma and the rigidity theorem are two faces of the same coefficient.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Classification for power-shaped witnesses]\label{thm:classification}
Let $(W,w)$ be a semiprime witness with $w(s) = s^k+c$ on odd primes, $k \ge 1$, $c \ne 0$.
Then simultaneously (i) $c(p^k+q^k) = W(pq)-(pq)^k-c^2$ for all distinct odd primes, hence the
factorization is recovered in polynomial time from $W(N)$ and $N$; and (ii) no
$P \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ reproduces $W$ on the odd semiprimes. That is, $(W,w)$ is a free witness.
\end{theorem}

\section{The prediction: divisor power sums}

\begin{lemma}
For $p$ prime, $\sigma_k(p) = 1+p^k$; and for distinct primes $p \ne q$,
$\sigma_k(pq) = (1+p^k)(1+q^k)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The divisors of $p$ are $1$ and $p$; $\sigma_k$ is multiplicative on coprime arguments and
distinct primes are coprime.
\end{proof}

Thus $\sigma_k$ is a semiprime witness with power-shaped local weight $x^k+1$, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:classification} applies verbatim.

\begin{theorem}[The predicted free witness]\label{thm:sigk}
For every $k \ge 1$ and distinct odd primes $p \ne q$ with $N = pq$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $p^k+q^k = \sigma_k(N)-N^k-1$;
\item $k=1$: $p+q = \sigma(N)-N-1$;
\item $k=2$: $(p+q)^2 + 1 + N^2 = \sigma_2(N) + 2N$, equivalently
\[
  p+q = \sqrt{\sigma_2(N)+2N-1-N^2},
\]
in which every quantity on the right is a function of $N$ and the witness value alone;
\item the factorization is determined: if $p'q' = N$ with $p' > 0$ and $(p'+q')^2$ equals the
right side of (3), then $\{p',q'\} = \{p,q\}$;
\item no integer polynomial computes $\sigma_k(pq)$ on the distinct-prime pairs.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
(1)--(3) are Theorem~\ref{thm:trace} and Corollary~\ref{cor:tracesq} with $a=c=1$, plus
$(p+q)^2 = p^2+q^2+2N$; the square root is exact because the radicand is $(p+q)^2$. (4) follows
from (3) and Theorem~\ref{thm:pair} using $u^2 = v^2$, $u,v \ge 0 \Rightarrow u=v$. (5) is
Theorem~\ref{thm:rigidity} with $c=1$; alternatively Proposition~\ref{prop:diff} with
$(N_1,N_2) = (33,15)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{table}[h]\centering
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
\toprule
$N = pq$ & $\sigma_2(N)$ & $(1+p^2)(1+q^2)$ & $p^2+q^2$ & $\sqrt{\sigma_2+2N-1-N^2}$\\
\midrule
$15 = 3\cdot5$   & $260$  & $10\cdot26$  & $34$  & $8 = 3+5$\\
$21 = 3\cdot7$   & $500$  & $10\cdot50$  & $58$  & $10 = 3+7$\\
$33 = 3\cdot11$  & $1220$ & $10\cdot122$ & $130$ & $14 = 3+11$\\
$35 = 5\cdot7$   & $1300$ & $26\cdot50$  & $74$  & $12 = 5+7$\\
$77 = 7\cdot11$  & $6100$ & $50\cdot122$ & $170$ & $18 = 7+11$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The predicted witness, verified numerically.}
\end{table}

\begin{proposition}[Sharpness of $k \ge 1$]
At $k = 0$ the witness degenerates: $\sigma_0(pq) = 4$ for all distinct primes, a constant,
hence a polynomial in $N$ carrying no factor information. The hypothesis $k \ge 1$ in
Theorem~\ref{thm:classification} cannot be dropped.
\end{proposition}

\section{Sealing: how much is a function of $N$ alone}

\begin{lemma}[Shift identity]\label{lem:shift}
For distinct primes $p \ne q$ and any $k$, with $N = pq$,
$\;\sigma_k(pq) = 2 + 2N^k - (p^k-1)(q^k-1)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[2-adic input]\label{lem:eight}
For odd $p$ and any $j$, $\;8 \mid p^{2j}-1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$p = 2m+1$ gives $p^2-1 = 4m(m+1)$ with $m(m+1)$ even, so $8 \mid p^2-1$; and
$x-1 \mid x^j-1$ with $x = p^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The truncation leaks nothing below $64$]\label{thm:seal64}
For every $j \ge 0$ and all distinct odd primes $p \ne q$ with $N = pq$,
\[
  \sigma_{2j}(N) \equiv 2 + 2N^{2j} \pmod{64}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:shift} the discrepancy is $(p^{2j}-1)(q^{2j}-1)$, and by
Lemma~\ref{lem:eight} each factor is divisible by $8$.
\end{proof}

Hence the low six bits of the witness are an explicit polynomial in $N$, and no separating pair
$N_1 \equiv N_2 \pmod {2^k}$ can exist for $k \le 6$: a brute-force search over all semiprimes
with both primes below $300$ (some $3\times10^5$ pairs) finds none, and the theorem explains why
the search \emph{must} fail.

\begin{theorem}[No function of $N \bmod 128$]\label{thm:sep128}
There is no function $g$ --- polynomial or arbitrary --- with
$\sigma_2(pq) \bmod 128 = g\bigl((pq)\bmod 128\bigr)$ for all distinct odd primes $p \ne q$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$N_1 = 15 = 3\cdot5$ and $N_2 = 527 = 17\cdot31$ satisfy $527 \equiv 15 \pmod{128}$, while
$\sigma_2(15) = 260 \equiv 4$ and $\sigma_2(527) = 290\cdot962 = 278980 \equiv 68 \pmod{128}$.
\end{proof}

This is strictly stronger than the polynomial barrier: it excludes every formula in the residue
of the modulus. Together with Theorem~\ref{thm:seal64} the 2-adic seal of $\sigma_2$ is located
exactly: transparent through $2^6$, opaque at $2^7$.

\begin{theorem}[The circle count is less sealed]
The same pair separates $C$ already at $32$: $C(15) = (3+1)(5-1) = 16$ and
$C(527) = (17-1)(31+1) = 512 \equiv 0 \pmod{32}$, while $527 \equiv 15 \pmod{32}$. Hence no
function of $N \bmod 32$ computes $C(N)\bmod 32$ on odd semiprimes.
\end{theorem}

Sealing is thus a quantitative attribute of a witness, not a binary one.

\section{Beyond semiprimes: the $\omega$-channel}\label{sec:omega}

\begin{theorem}[Product formula]\label{thm:prod}
For squarefree $N$, $\;\sigma_k(N) = \prod_{p \mid N}(1+p^k)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:localval}
For an odd prime $p$ and any $j$, $\;\vtwo(1+p^{2j}) = 1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:eight}, $p^{2j} = 1+8t$, so $1+p^{2j} = 2(4t+1)$ with $4t+1$ odd.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The $\omega$-channel]\label{thm:omega}
For odd squarefree $N$ and every $j \ge 0$, $\;\vtwo\bigl(\sigma_{2j}(N)\bigr) = \omega(N)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:prod} the witness is a product over $p \mid N$; valuations add; each term
contributes $1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:localval}; there are $\omega(N)$ terms.
\end{proof}

On semiprimes the valuation is the constant $2$, which is why the channel is invisible in the
two-factor setting. Numerically: $\sigma_2(15) = 2^2\cdot65$, $\sigma_2(105) = 2^3\cdot1625$,
$\sigma_2(1155) = 2^4\cdot99125$, $\sigma_2(15015) = 2^5\cdot8425625$, for $\omega = 2,3,4,5$.
The slogan ``one factor-secret coordinate per witness'' is therefore an artifact of the
semiprime restriction: the multiplicative structure of the aggregate carries $\omega(N)$ in its
valuation, independently of the trace channel.

\section{The boundary of the class}

\subsection{Truncation}

\begin{theorem}[Truncation leaves the class]
Let $f(x) = \ind{2(x \bmod 15) < 15}$. Then $f \notin \Split(3,5)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:rankone} to $x=0$, $y=1$, $z=6$, $w=10$, whose CRT coordinates are
$(0,0),(1,1),(0,1),(1,0)$, so the crossing conditions hold. Rank-one demands
$f(0)f(1) = f(6)f(10)$, i.e.\ $1 = 0$.
\end{proof}

The value grid with rows indexed by $x \bmod 3$ and columns by $x \bmod 5$ is
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4\\\hline
0 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0\\
1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 1\\
2 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0
\end{array}
\]
whose top-left $2\times2$ block has rank two.

\begin{theorem}[Character-like weights stay inside]
For coprime $m,n$, the indicator $x \mapsto \ind{x^2 \equiv 1 \bmod mn}$ lies in $\Split(m,n)$,
with $A(a) = \ind{a^2 \equiv 1 \bmod m}$ and $B(b) = \ind{b^2\equiv1 \bmod n}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$x^2 \equiv 1 \bmod mn$ iff $x^2 \equiv 1$ mod $m$ and mod $n$; the indicator of a conjunction
is the product of indicators; and $x^2 \bmod m$ depends only on $x \bmod m$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Phases: splitting holds, locality fails}

It is often asserted that exponential phase weights $y \mapsto e^{2\pi i f(y)/N}$ fail because
such phases do not decompose through the CRT, only group characters doing so. \emph{This
justification is false as stated.}

\begin{theorem}[Phases do split]
Let $m,n$ be coprime with B\'ezout data $un+vm = 1$. Then $x = (ux)n + (vx)m$ for every integer
$x$, hence $x/(mn) = ux/m + vx/n$ in $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ and
\[
  e^{2\pi i x/(mn)} = e^{2\pi i (ux)/m}\cdot e^{2\pi i (vx)/n}
\]
exactly, with no error term.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The twist depends on the co-modulus]
In that decomposition the local weight at $m$ is $y \mapsto e^{2\pi i uy/m}$ with
$u \equiv n^{-1} \pmod m$: the twist is a function of the \emph{other} modulus. Modulo $7$,
$3^{-1} = 5$ while $5^{-1} = 3$, and the induced local weights $y \mapsto 5y$ and
$y \mapsto 3y$ on $\mathbb{Z}/7$ differ already at $y = 1$. Consistently with B\'ezout,
$5\cdot3 + (-2)\cdot7 = 1$ and $3\cdot5+(-2)\cdot7 = 1$.
\end{theorem}

Hence a phase witness factors, but its local factor at $p$ is not a function of $p$ alone: it
depends on $q$ through the modular inverse. The class boundary is drawn by \emph{locality}, not
by splitting.

\subsection{Non-separability does not buy a closed form}

\begin{theorem}
The half-plane count $H$, the non-CRT-separable companion of the circle count, is also not a
polynomial in $N$: $H(15) = 4$, $H(35) = 6$, and $20 \nmid 2$; apply
Proposition~\ref{prop:diff}.
\end{theorem}

The two barriers --- non-separability and non-polynomiality --- are therefore logically
independent properties of a counting aggregate.

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Trace-channel factorization]
Input: odd semiprime $N$ and witness value $W$ with affine-power data $(a,k,c)$. Compute
$t = (W - a^2N^k - c^2)/(ac)$; set $s = t$ if $k=1$ and $s = \sqrt{t+2N}$ if $k=2$; compute
$d = \sqrt{s^2-4N}$; return $\{(s-d)/2,(s+d)/2\}$. Cost: $O(1)$ arithmetic operations plus two
integer square roots, i.e.\ $\tilde O(\log^2 N)$ bit operations.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Rank-one membership test]
Input: coprime $m,n$ and a weight $f$ on $\mathbb{Z}/mn$ over a field with $f(0)\ne0$. For each
$x$ form $z = \crt(x \bmod m,0)$, $w = \crt(0,x\bmod n)$ and test $f(x)f(0) = f(z)f(w)$; on
success return $A(a) = f(\crt(a,0))$, $B(b) = f(\crt(0,b))/f(0)$, else return the violating
quadruple. Cost: $O(mn)$ field operations in the anchored form.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[2-adic sealing scan]
Input: prime bound $P$, modulus $2^k$, witness $W$. Enumerate semiprimes $N = pq$ with
$3 \le p < q < P$, bucket by $N \bmod 2^k$, and report any bucket containing two moduli with
distinct $W(N) \bmod 2^k$. Theorem~\ref{thm:seal64} predicts empty output for $\sigma_{2j}$ at
every $k \le 6$; Theorem~\ref{thm:sep128} predicts a hit at $k = 7$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[$\omega$ extraction]
Input: odd squarefree $N$ and the value $\sigma_{2j}(N)$. Return $\vtwo(\sigma_{2j}(N))$ by
repeated halving; the output equals $\omega(N)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:omega}.
\end{algorithmbox}

\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{A design criterion.} Any protocol whose security rests on the difficulty of
extracting structure from a modulus should avoid publishing aggregates whose summand weight is
CRT-multiplicative with a non-polynomial local factor. Theorem~\ref{thm:fourpoint} makes this
checkable: form the CRT grid of the weight and test rank one on the quadruples anchored at $0$.

\paragraph{Unification with predictive content.} Before the classification there were nine
coincidences and no criterion. Now there is a definition, a decidable membership test, a
completeness theorem with three channels, a rigidity theorem, a validated prediction, a
delimited boundary and a quantitative seal.

\paragraph{A correction to the record.} The exclusion of phase witnesses was justified by the
claim that phases do not decompose through the CRT. They do, exactly. The real obstruction is
that the B\'ezout twist depends on the co-modulus, so the local factor is not a function of one
prime. The distinction matters for anyone attempting to enlarge the class.

\paragraph{What is not established.} That the $\Theta(N)$ aggregation cost is \emph{necessary}.
That statement is equivalent to the hardness of factoring. The classification characterizes the
mechanism precisely; it does not prove the barrier unconditionally.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Exact 2-adic sealing threshold]
For odd distinct primes $p,q$ and $k = 2j$, write $v = \vtwo(k)+2$. Then $\sigma_k(pq) \bmod
2^{2v}$ is a polynomial function of $N \bmod 2^{2v}$, and there exist semiprimes
$N_1 \equiv N_2 \pmod{2^{2v+1}}$ with $\sigma_k(N_1) \not\equiv \sigma_k(N_2) \pmod{2^{2v+1}}$.
The leakage is governed by $\sigma_k(N) = 2+2N^k-(p^k-1)(q^k-1)$: for even $k$ and odd $p$ the
valuation of $p^k-1$ is exactly $\vtwo(k)+2$ by lifting the exponent, so the correction vanishes
precisely below $2^{2v}$. The case $k=2$ is Theorems~\ref{thm:seal64} and~\ref{thm:sep128}.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Every witness leaks $\omega(N)$]
Let $F$ be a CRT-multiplicative witness whose local weight satisfies $w(p) = u\cdot m(p)$ with a
fixed prime power $u$ and $m(p)$ coprime to $u$ for all odd primes $p$. Then
$v_u(W(N)) = \omega(N)$ for all odd squarefree $N$. The case $u = 2$, $w(p) = 1+p^{2j}$ is
Theorem~\ref{thm:omega}.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Decidability, sharply]
For a weight $f$ on $\mathbb{Z}/mn$ with values in a field, membership in the
CRT-multiplicative class is decided by $O(m^2n^2)$ field operations, and no smaller test
suffices: for every $(m,n)$ there is a weight failing exactly one rank-one quadruple.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Locality characterizes the phase boundary]
Formalize ``local weight is a function of one prime'' as independence of the family of
factorizations from the co-modulus, and prove that a weight admits a co-modulus-independent
splitting if and only if it is a product of Dirichlet characters times a multiplicative
function of the residue.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Quantitative sealing as an invariant]
Attach to each witness the largest $k$ such that $W(N) \bmod 2^k$ is a function of
$N \bmod 2^k$ on odd semiprimes ($6$ for $\sigma_{2j}$, $4$ for the circle count). This
invariant is computable from the local weight alone --- specifically from the 2-adic expansion
of $w(p)-w(1)$ --- and is monotone under the operations generating new members from old.
\end{conjecture}

\section{Conclusion}

The free-witness family is one mechanism: a non-polynomial, CRT-multiplicative local weight
aggregated over a CRT-separable domain. Layer one is a theorem, and its converse over a field is
a four-point test making class membership decidable. The Trace Lemma shows that the aggregate
hands over a power sum $p^k+q^k$, and that this single coordinate, through any of three complete
channels, is the factorization. The rigidity theorem shows no polynomial in $N$ can shadow such
a witness for any $k \ge 1$, and localizes the obstruction in the constant term of the local
weight. The classification predicted the divisor power sums as new members, and they are. Its
boundary is drawn twice: truncation exits by failing rank one; phase weights --- which,
contrary to the standard account, do split --- exit by failing locality. Finally, the semiprime
picture was hiding a second channel: the 2-adic valuation of the witness counts the prime
factors of the modulus. What remains open is whether the $\Theta(N)$ cost of aggregating
without the factors is necessary --- the same hard question as always.

\end{document}

"""
Numerical demonstrations for the CRT-multiplicative free-witness classification
and the Trace Lemma.

Everything is self-contained: no imports beyond the standard library, all helper
functions inlined, full type hints.

The script demonstrates, in order:

  1. The CRT grid and the product formula for split weights (Layer 1).
  2. The rank-one criterion: which weights split, which do not.
  3. The Trace Lemma and factorization from a single scalar.
  4. The predicted witness sigma_k, and the explicit trace formula at k = 2.
  5. The polynomial barrier via the difference test, and the rigidity identity.
  6. The 2-adic sealing dichotomy: nothing below 64, separation at 128.
  7. The omega-channel: v_2(sigma_{2j}(N)) = omega(N).
  8. The phase boundary: phases split, but the Bezout twist is non-local.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from math import isqrt
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Elementary number theory helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    """Deterministic trial-division primality test (adequate for demo sizes)."""
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return n == 2
    d = 3
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
        d += 2
    return True


def primes_up_to(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes < limit, by a simple sieve of Eratosthenes."""
    sieve = [True] * max(limit, 2)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = False
    for i in range(2, isqrt(limit - 1) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            for j in range(i * i, limit, i):
                sieve[j] = False
    return [i for i, ok in enumerate(sieve) if ok]


def divisors(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """All positive divisors of n, ascending."""
    small: List[int] = []
    large: List[int] = []
    d = 1
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            small.append(d)
            if d != n // d:
                large.append(n // d)
        d += 1
    return small + large[::-1]


def sigma_k(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """Divisor power sum sigma_k(n) = sum over d | n of d^k."""
    return sum(d ** k for d in divisors(n))


def prime_factors(n: int) -> List[int]:
    """Distinct prime factors of n, ascending."""
    out: List[int] = []
    m = n
    d = 2
    while d * d <= m:
        if m % d == 0:
            out.append(d)
            while m % d == 0:
                m //= d
        d += 1
    if m > 1:
        out.append(m)
    return out


def omega(n: int) -> int:
    """Number of distinct prime factors of n."""
    return len(prime_factors(n))


def v2(n: int) -> int:
    """2-adic valuation of a nonzero integer."""
    if n == 0:
        raise ValueError("v2(0) is undefined")
    e = 0
    while n % 2 == 0:
        n //= 2
        e += 1
    return e


def egcd(a: int, b: int) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Extended Euclid: returns (g, x, y) with a*x + b*y = g = gcd(a, b)."""
    if b == 0:
        return (a, 1, 0)
    g, x, y = egcd(b, a % b)
    return (g, y, x - (a // b) * y)


def crt(a: int, m: int, b: int, n: int) -> int:
    """The unique x in [0, m*n) with x = a (mod m) and x = b (mod n), gcd(m,n)=1."""
    g, u, v = egcd(m, n)
    if g != 1:
        raise ValueError("moduli must be coprime")
    return (a * v * n + b * u * m) % (m * n)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The circle count C(N) = #{(x,y) : x^2 + y^2 = 1 mod N}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def circle_count(n: int) -> int:
    """Brute-force count of points on the modular unit circle mod n."""
    squares: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for x in range(n):
        s = (x * x) % n
        squares[s] = squares.get(s, 0) + 1
    total = 0
    for x in range(n):
        need = (1 - x * x) % n
        total += squares.get(need, 0)
    return total


def circle_local_weight(p: int) -> int:
    """Local weight of the circle count at an odd prime: p - chi_p(-1)."""
    return p - 1 if p % 4 == 1 else p + 1


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The CRT grid and the product formula (Layer 1)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def crt_grid(m: int, n: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    """The m x n grid whose (a, b) entry is the residue mod m*n with those coordinates."""
    return [[crt(a, m, b, n) for b in range(n)] for a in range(m)]


def aggregate_of_split_weight(
    m: int, n: int, a_fun: Callable[[int], int], b_fun: Callable[[int], int]
) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Return (direct sum over [0, mn), product of the two local sums)."""
    direct = sum(a_fun(x % m) * b_fun(x % n) for x in range(m * n))
    product = sum(a_fun(a) for a in range(m)) * sum(b_fun(b) for b in range(n))
    return direct, product


def demo_layer_one() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("1. THE CRT GRID AND THE PRODUCT FORMULA (Layer 1)")
    print("=" * 78)
    m, n = 3, 5
    grid = crt_grid(m, n)
    print(f"\nResidues mod {m*n}, indexed by (x mod {m}, x mod {n}):\n")
    header = "      " + "".join(f"b={b:<4}" for b in range(n))
    print(header)
    for a in range(m):
        print(f" a={a} |" + "".join(f"{grid[a][b]:<6}" for b in range(n)))

    # A split weight: A(a) = a + 1, B(b) = 2b - 3.
    a_fun: Callable[[int], int] = lambda a: a + 1
    b_fun: Callable[[int], int] = lambda b: 2 * b - 3
    direct, product = aggregate_of_split_weight(m, n, a_fun, b_fun)
    print(f"\nSplit weight f(x) = A(x mod 3) * B(x mod 5) with A(a)=a+1, B(b)=2b-3:")
    print(f"  sum over the whole grid  = {direct}")
    print(f"  (sum of A)*(sum of B)    = {product}")
    print(f"  identical: {direct == product}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The rank-one criterion
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def rank_one_violation(
    m: int, n: int, f: Callable[[int], int]
) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int, int, int]]:
    """Search crossed CRT quadruples for a violation of f(x)f(y) = f(z)f(w).

    Returns the first violating quadruple (x, y, z, w), or None if the weight
    passes every test (hence splits, when f never vanishes over a field).
    """
    mn = m * n
    for x in range(mn):
        for y in range(mn):
            z = crt(x % m, m, y % n, n)
            w = crt(y % m, m, x % n, n)
            if f(x) * f(y) != f(z) * f(w):
                return (x, y, z, w)
    return None


def sqrt_one_weight(modulus: int) -> Callable[[int], int]:
    """Indicator of x^2 = 1 (mod modulus): the character-like CIRC/BQF weight."""
    return lambda x: 1 if (x * x) % modulus == 1 % modulus else 0


def trunc_weight(x: int) -> int:
    """Truncated (half-plane) weight mod 15: 1 on the lower half of the interval."""
    return 1 if 2 * (x % 15) < 15 else 0


def demo_rank_one() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("2. THE RANK-ONE CRITERION: WHO SPLITS AND WHO DOES NOT")
    print("=" * 78)

    print("\nValue grid of the truncated weight [2(x mod 15) < 15]:\n")
    grid = crt_grid(3, 5)
    print("      " + "".join(f"b={b:<4}" for b in range(5)))
    for a in range(3):
        print(f" a={a} |" + "".join(f"{trunc_weight(grid[a][b]):<6}" for b in range(5)))

    bad = rank_one_violation(3, 5, trunc_weight)
    print(f"\n  truncated weight  -> violating quadruple {bad}")
    if bad is not None:
        x, y, z, w = bad
        print(
            f"     f({x})*f({y}) = {trunc_weight(x)*trunc_weight(y)}   "
            f"but f({z})*f({w}) = {trunc_weight(z)*trunc_weight(w)}   => does NOT split"
        )

    good = rank_one_violation(3, 5, sqrt_one_weight(15))
    print(f"  sqrt-of-one weight -> violating quadruple {good}  => SPLITS")

    print("\nThe sqrt-of-one grid is literally an outer product:")
    row = [1 if (a * a) % 3 == 1 else 0 for a in range(3)]
    col = [1 if (b * b) % 5 == 1 else 0 for b in range(5)]
    print(f"  row profile [a^2=1 mod 3] = {row}")
    print(f"  col profile [b^2=1 mod 5] = {col}")
    ok = all(
        sqrt_one_weight(15)(grid[a][b]) == row[a] * col[b]
        for a in range(3)
        for b in range(5)
    )
    print(f"  grid equals outer product: {ok}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3-4. The Trace Lemma, and the predicted witness sigma_k
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def factor_from_trace(n: int, s: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Given N = pq and the trace s = p + q, return (p, q) with p <= q."""
    disc = s * s - 4 * n
    d = isqrt(disc)
    if d * d != disc:
        raise ValueError("discriminant is not a perfect square")
    return ((s - d) // 2, (s + d) // 2)


def trace_from_sigma2(n: int) -> int:
    """p + q = sqrt(sigma_2(N) + 2N - 1 - N^2) for an odd semiprime N = pq."""
    radicand = sigma_k(n, 2) + 2 * n - 1 - n * n
    s = isqrt(radicand)
    if s * s != radicand:
        raise ValueError("radicand is not a perfect square")
    return s


def factor_via_sigma2(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Full factorization of an odd semiprime from the single scalar sigma_2(N)."""
    return factor_from_trace(n, trace_from_sigma2(n))


def demo_trace_lemma() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("3. THE TRACE LEMMA: ONE SCALAR, BOTH PRIMES")
    print("=" * 78)

    print("\nCIRC (Blum pairs, p = q = 3 mod 4):  p + q = C(N) - N - 1\n")
    print(f"  {'N = p*q':<14}{'C(N)':>8}{'C(N)-N-1':>12}{'p+q':>8}")
    for p, q in [(3, 7), (3, 11), (3, 19), (7, 11), (7, 19)]:
        n = p * q
        c = circle_count(n)
        print(f"  {f'{n} = {p}*{q}':<14}{c:>8}{c - n - 1:>12}{p + q:>8}")

    print("\nThe local product formula C(pq) = (p - chi_p(-1))(q - chi_q(-1)):\n")
    for p, q in [(3, 5), (3, 7), (5, 13), (17, 31)]:
        n = p * q
        print(
            f"  C({n:<5}) = {circle_count(n):<7} "
            f"= {circle_local_weight(p)} * {circle_local_weight(q)} "
            f"= {circle_local_weight(p) * circle_local_weight(q)}"
        )

    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("4. THE PREDICTED WITNESS sigma_k, AND THE EXPLICIT TRACE FORMULA")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("\n  sigma_k(pq) = (1 + p^k)(1 + q^k),   p^k + q^k = sigma_k(N) - N^k - 1")
    print("  k = 2:  p + q = sqrt(sigma_2(N) + 2N - 1 - N^2)\n")
    print(
        f"  {'N = p*q':<15}{'sigma_2(N)':>12}{'(1+p^2)(1+q^2)':>17}"
        f"{'p^2+q^2':>10}{'recovered {p,q}':>20}"
    )
    for p, q in [(3, 5), (3, 7), (3, 11), (5, 7), (7, 11), (17, 31), (101, 103)]:
        n = p * q
        s2 = sigma_k(n, 2)
        local = (1 + p * p) * (1 + q * q)
        power_sum = s2 - n * n - 1
        rec = factor_via_sigma2(n)
        assert s2 == local and power_sum == p * p + q * q and rec == (p, q)
        print(
            f"  {f'{n} = {p}*{q}':<15}{s2:>12}{local:>17}{power_sum:>10}"
            f"{str(rec):>20}"
        )

    print("\n  Higher exponents, same mechanism (p^k + q^k = sigma_k(N) - N^k - 1):\n")
    p, q = 13, 17
    n = p * q
    for k in range(1, 6):
        lhs = p ** k + q ** k
        rhs = sigma_k(n, k) - n ** k - 1
        print(f"    k={k}:  p^k+q^k = {lhs:<14} sigma_k - N^k - 1 = {rhs:<14} equal={lhs == rhs}")

    print("\n  Sharpness at k = 0:  sigma_0(pq) = 4 always, a constant with no secret.")
    print(
        "    "
        + ", ".join(f"sigma_0({p*q})={sigma_k(p*q, 0)}" for p, q in [(3, 5), (3, 7), (7, 11)])
    )


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. The polynomial barrier
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def difference_test(w: Callable[[int], int], n1: int, n2: int) -> bool:
    """True if (n1 - n2) does NOT divide W(n1) - W(n2): no polynomial formula exists."""
    return (w(n1) - w(n2)) % (n1 - n2) != 0


def demo_polynomial_barrier() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("5. THE POLYNOMIAL BARRIER")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("\n  For any P in Z[X]:  a - b divides P(a) - P(b).")
    print("  A single violating pair therefore rules out every polynomial formula.\n")

    for name, w, n1, n2 in [
        ("circle count C", circle_count, 21, 15),
        ("sigma_2", lambda n: sigma_k(n, 2), 33, 15),
        ("sigma_1", lambda n: sigma_k(n, 1), 33, 15),
    ]:
        d_n = n1 - n2
        d_w = w(n1) - w(n2)
        print(
            f"  {name:<16} W({n1})-W({n2}) = {d_w:<8} {n1}-{n2} = {d_n:<4} "
            f"divides? {d_w % d_n == 0}    -> non-polynomial: {difference_test(w, n1, n2)}"
        )

    print("\n  Rigidity (the structural argument).  A polynomial formula would force")
    print("  P(3X) = (3^k+c)(X^k+c) and P(5X) = (5^k+c)(X^k+c), hence two values of")
    print("  P(30) whose equality reduces to c*(10^k+3^k) = c*(6^k+5^k):\n")
    print(f"    {'k':>3}{'10^k+3^k':>12}{'6^k+5^k':>12}   equal?")
    for k in range(1, 8):
        left = 10 ** k + 3 ** k
        right = 6 ** k + 5 ** k
        print(f"    {k:>3}{left:>12}{right:>12}   {left == right}")
    print("\n  Never equal for k >= 1, so c = 0: only the information-free weight x^k")
    print("  admits a polynomial closed form.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. The 2-adic sealing dichotomy
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def sealing_scan(
    w: Callable[[int], int], prime_bound: int, modulus: int
) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Search odd semiprimes N < prime_bound^2 for N1 = N2 (mod modulus) with
    differing witness residues.  Returns the first separating pair, or None."""
    ps = [p for p in primes_up_to(prime_bound) if p != 2]
    buckets: Dict[Tuple[int, int], int] = {}
    for i, p in enumerate(ps):
        for q in ps[i + 1 :]:
            n = p * q
            key = (n % modulus, w(n) % modulus)
            residue = n % modulus
            for (r, val), seen in list(buckets.items()):
                if r == residue and val != key[1]:
                    return (seen, n)
            buckets.setdefault(key, n)
    return None


def demo_sealing() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("6. THE 2-ADIC SEALING DICHOTOMY")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("\n  Theorem: sigma_{2j}(N) = 2 + 2N^{2j} (mod 64) for all odd semiprimes.")
    print("  Check across exponents and semiprimes:\n")
    ok = True
    for j in [1, 2, 3]:
        for p, q in [(3, 5), (3, 7), (5, 11), (17, 31), (23, 29)]:
            n = p * q
            lhs = sigma_k(n, 2 * j) % 64
            rhs = (2 + 2 * pow(n, 2 * j)) % 64
            ok = ok and lhs == rhs
    print(f"    sigma_2j(N) = 2 + 2N^2j (mod 64) in every case tested: {ok}")

    print("\n  Consequently no separating pair can exist below 2^7.  Scan (primes < 300):\n")
    print(f"    {'modulus':>10}{'sigma_2':>26}{'circle count':>26}")
    for k in range(3, 9):
        mod = 2 ** k
        s_pair = sealing_scan(lambda n: sigma_k(n, 2), 120, mod)
        c_pair = sealing_scan(circle_count, 60, mod)
        print(
            f"    {mod:>10}{str(s_pair) if s_pair else 'none':>26}"
            f"{str(c_pair) if c_pair else 'none':>26}"
        )

    print("\n  The canonical separation at 128:  15 = 3*5 and 527 = 17*31.\n")
    for n in (15, 527):
        print(
            f"    N = {n:<5} N mod 128 = {n % 128:<5} "
            f"sigma_2(N) = {sigma_k(n, 2):<8} sigma_2 mod 128 = {sigma_k(n, 2) % 128}"
        )
    print("\n  Same pair separates the circle count already at 32:\n")
    for n in (15, 527):
        c = circle_count(n)
        print(
            f"    N = {n:<5} N mod 32 = {n % 32:<5} "
            f"C(N) = {c:<8} C(N) mod 32 = {c % 32}"
        )
    print("\n  => sigma_2 conceals six bits; the circle count only four.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. The omega-channel
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_omega_channel() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("7. THE OMEGA-CHANNEL: v_2(sigma_{2j}(N)) = omega(N)")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("\n  Each local factor 1 + p^{2j} = 2 * odd, so the valuation counts the primes.\n")
    print(f"  {'N':>8}  {'factorization':<22}{'sigma_2(N)':>14}{'v_2':>6}{'omega':>7}")
    for n in [15, 33, 105, 1155, 15015, 255255, 3 * 5 * 7 * 11 * 13 * 17 * 19]:
        fs = prime_factors(n)
        s2 = sigma_k(n, 2)
        print(
            f"  {n:>8}  {'*'.join(map(str, fs)):<22}{s2:>14}{v2(s2):>6}{omega(n):>7}"
        )
    print("\n  Invisible on semiprimes (the valuation is the constant 2); a genuine")
    print("  second secret in general.  Same for higher even exponents:\n")
    for j in [1, 2, 3]:
        n = 1155
        print(f"    j={j}:  v_2(sigma_{2*j}({n})) = {v2(sigma_k(n, 2*j))}   omega({n}) = {omega(n)}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. The phase boundary
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_phase_boundary() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("8. THE PHASE BOUNDARY: SPLITTING HOLDS, LOCALITY FAILS")
    print("=" * 78)
    m, n = 7, 3
    g, u, v = egcd(n, m)  # u*n + v*m = 1
    print(f"\n  Bezout for (m, n) = ({m}, {n}):  {u}*{n} + {v}*{m} = {u*n + v*m}")
    print(f"  So x = ({u}x)*{n} + ({v}x)*{m} for every x, i.e. the phase index splits exactly:")
    ok = all(x == (u * x) * n + (v * x) * m for x in range(-20, 21))
    print(f"    identity x = (u x) n + (v x) m holds on a test range: {ok}")

    print("\n  But the local twist at m is u = n^{-1} mod m, a function of the OTHER modulus:")
    for other in (3, 5):
        _, uu, _ = egcd(other, 7)
        print(f"    with co-modulus n = {other}:  twist u = {other}^(-1) mod 7 = {uu % 7}")
    print("\n  The two induced local weights y -> 5y and y -> 3y on Z/7 differ:")
    print(f"    y=1:  5*1 mod 7 = {5 % 7},  3*1 mod 7 = {3 % 7}   -> different functions")
    print("\n  So a phase witness factors, but its 'local' factor is not a function of")
    print("  one prime alone.  The class boundary is locality, not splitting.")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> None:
    demo_layer_one()
    demo_rank_one()
    demo_trace_lemma()
    demo_polynomial_barrier()
    demo_sealing()
    demo_omega_channel()
    demo_phase_boundary()
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print("All demonstrations completed.")
    print("=" * 78)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

It builds the Chinese Remainder grid for 15 = 3 x 5 and confirms that a split weight's total equals the product of its two axis totals; runs the rank-one test on the character-like square-root-of-one weight (which splits) and the truncated half-interval weight (which fails on the rectangle 0, 1, 6, 10); verifies the trace recovery p + q = C(N) - N - 1 for the modular circle count on Blum pairs and the local product formula C(pq) = (p - chi_p(-1))(q - chi_q(-1)); confirms the predicted divisor-power witness sigma_k(pq) = (1 + p^k)(1 + q^k) together with the explicit trace formula p + q = sqrt(sigma_2(N) + 2N - 1 - N^2) and full factor recovery; exhibits the polynomial barrier through the difference test and tabulates the rigidity separation 10^k + 3^k versus 6^k + 5^k; scans semiprimes for two-adic separations, finding none below 128 for sigma_2 and exhibiting the canonical pair 15 versus 527; reads the number of prime factors off the two-adic valuation of the witness; and demonstrates that exponential phases do split through the Chinese Remainder Theorem while their Bezout twist is non-local.
